subject: chemistry
question_text: Derive the relation between Kp and Kc for an equilibrium reaction.

verification.note: Chapter 7 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.75-79), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter prints NO Long Answer section, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book asks this content twice — as its three-star VSAQ 2 (state the relation) and as its unstarred SAQ 10 (derive it) — so the 2-mark form is authored as a cut of this card. The book's SAQ answer derives the relation only for the ammonia equilibrium N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, reaching Kp = Kc(RT)⁻²; this card derives the general form for aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, which is what 'for an equilibrium reaction' asks, and its Δn cases match the book's VSAQ answer.

page_header: Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 4 marks

steps.label: Kp and Kc expressions
lines: where pA, pB, pC, pD are the partial
steps.why: Kc and Kp describe the same equilibrium with two different measures — concentration and partial pressure — so the derivation starts by writing both expressions for one general reaction.
common_mistakes: Writing the reactants on top. Products go in the numerator of both expressions.
Dropping the powers a, b, c, d. Each term is raised to its coefficient in the balanced equation.
steps.memory_tip: Products over reactants, each raised to its own coefficient — same shape for Kc and Kp.
steps.margin_note: One general reaction, two expressions. This is the frame the marks hang on.

steps.label: Replace pressure by concentration
lines: For an ideal gas, PV = nRT, so
The partial pressure of each gas equals its
steps.why: The ideal gas equation is the bridge between the two measures: n/V is the molar concentration, so every partial pressure is that concentration times RT. This one line makes the substitution possible.
common_mistakes: Writing p = nRT and forgetting the volume. It is p = (n/V)RT.
Using Celsius temperature. T in PV = nRT is the absolute temperature in kelvin.
steps.memory_tip: n over V is concentration, so pressure is concentration times RT.
steps.margin_note: The whole derivation rests on p = CRT — write it as its own line.

steps.label: Substitute and collect RT
lines: Substituting the partial pressures into Kp:
steps.why: Every substituted pressure brings one factor of RT with the same power as its concentration, so the RT factors collect into one power: products contribute c + d, reactants a + b, and the difference is Δn.
common_mistakes: Adding the RT powers instead of subtracting. The reactant power (a + b) is subtracted from the product power (c + d).
Losing a power of RT by substituting into only some of the pressure terms.
steps.memory_tip: Each gas carries one RT to its own power. Products minus reactants leaves RT to the Δn.
steps.margin_note: Show the exponent subtraction — it is the algebra this mark checks.

steps.label: The relation and the sign of Δn
lines: Δn = moles of gaseous products − moles of
If Δn = 0, Kp = Kc. If Δn is positive,
Kp > Kc. If Δn is negative, Kp < Kc.
steps.why: The boxed relation is the result, but Δn must be defined with it — products minus reactants, gases only — because the sign of Δn decides whether Kp is larger than, equal to or smaller than Kc.
common_mistakes: Writing Δn as reactants minus products. It is gaseous products minus gaseous reactants.
Counting solids or liquids in Δn. Only gaseous moles are counted.
Leaving out the three sign cases.
steps.memory_tip: Δn reads left to right as the reaction is written: products first, minus reactants, gases only.
steps.margin_note: Box the relation; the Δn definition and sign cases sit under it.

insider_note: Asked at both lengths — the two-mark form asks for the relation with every symbol named, the four-mark form asks for the derivation. The sign of Δn is where the marks are lost: write products minus reactants, gases only, every time.
